hints: Think about what happens to shared electrons when two bonded atoms have different abilities to attract electrons.
walkthrough:
Picture unequal sharing**
Imagine $\text{H-F}$ as a tug of war for electrons. Fluorine pulls much harder than hydrogen, so the shared pair spends more time near fluorine. That means one end becomes slightly negative and the other slightly positive.

Final answer: A polar bond is one in which the centres of positive and negative charge do not coincide, so electron distribution is unequal and the bonded atoms carry partial charges, $\delta+$ and $\delta-$.

hints: Compare the boiling points in the table, $19^{\circ}\text{C}$ for HF against $-85$ to $-35^{\circ}\text{C}$ for the others, and ask what extra strong force only HF can have.
Link the strength of intermolecular forces to the energy needed to separate molecules when boiling.
walkthrough:
Spot the odd one out**
Look at the table. HCl, HBr and HI boil at $-85$, $-67$ and $-35^{\circ}\text{C}$, but HF boils at $+19^{\circ}\text{C}$. That huge jump tells you something extra is holding HF molecules together.

Name the stronger force and link to energy**
In HF, hydrogen is bonded directly to highly electronegative fluorine, so $\text{H}^{\delta+}...\text{F}^{\delta-}$ hydrogen bonds form between molecules. These are far stronger than the ordinary permanent dipole-dipole forces in the other hydrogen halides. Boiling only separates molecules, it does not break covalent $\text{H-X}$ bonds, so more thermal energy is needed to overcome the hydrogen bonds in HF.

Final answer: HF has hydrogen bonding between molecules, which is much stronger than the permanent dipole-dipole forces between molecules of HCl, HBr and HI.
More energy is required to overcome these stronger forces, so HF has a much higher boiling point.

hints: Use the H-X bond energy data, $562$ down to $299\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$, to state the trend in how easily the molecules decompose on heating.
Think about what happens to halogen atomic size and shielding from F to I and how this affects orbital overlap with hydrogen.
Connect weaker H-X bonds to less energy needed to break them.
walkthrough:
State the stability trend from data**
Thermal stability means resistance to breaking apart on heating. The bond energies fall steadily: $562$ for $\text{H-F}$, $431$ for $\text{H-Cl}$, $366$ for $\text{H-Br}$, $299\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$ for $\text{H-I}$. So HF is most stable and HI decomposes most easily.

Explain why bonds get weaker**
Picture the halogen getting bigger from F to I. The outer electron is further out and more shielded, so overlap between the hydrogen $1s$ orbital and the halogen $p$ orbital becomes longer and weaker.

Link bond strength to heat needed**
Breaking $\text{H-X}$ needs energy equal to the bond energy. A smaller bond energy means less heating is required to split the molecule into $\text{H}_2$ and $\text{X}_2$, so stability falls from HF to HI.

Final answer: Thermal stability decreases from HF to HI down Group 17.
Down the group the halogen atom becomes larger with more shielding, so H-X orbital overlap becomes poorer.
H-X bond energy decreases, so less energy is needed to break the H-X bond on heating.

hints: Recall that a Bronsted-Lowry base accepts $\text{H}^{+}$ and its conjugate acid is formed by adding one $\text{H}^{+}$ to it.
Follow the $\text{H}^{+}$ in $\text{H}_{2}\text{SO}_{4} + \text{NaCl} \rightarrow \text{NaHSO}_{4} + \text{HCl}$ to see which chloride containing species gains the proton.
walkthrough:
Track the proton**
Write the ionic change: $\text{H}_{2}\text{SO}_{4} + \text{Cl}^{-} \rightarrow \text{HSO}_{4}^{-} + \text{HCl}$. The $\text{H}_{2}\text{SO}_{4}$ loses $\text{H}^{+}$, so it acts as acid. The $\text{Cl}^{-}$ gains that $\text{H}^{+}$, so it acts as base.

Pair base with its conjugate acid**
A conjugate pair differs by exactly one $\text{H}^{+}$. Here $\text{Cl}^{-}$ plus $\text{H}^{+}$ gives $\text{HCl}$. So $\text{Cl}^{-}$ is base-I and $\text{HCl}$ is acid-II. The other pair is $\text{H}_{2}\text{SO}_{4}$ and $\text{HSO}_{4}^{-}$.

Final answer: Bronsted-Lowry base = $\text{Cl}^{-}$ (from NaCl), conjugate acid = $\text{HCl}$.
$\text{Cl}^{-}$ accepts a proton from $\text{H}_{2}\text{SO}_{4}$ to form $\text{HCl}$, which has one more $\text{H}^{+}$ than the base.

hints: Remember that concentrated $\text{H}_{2}\text{SO}_{4}$ is not just an acid, it is also a strong oxidising agent toward good reducing agents like $\text{I}^{-}$.
Think about what happens to any HI first formed when it meets excess concentrated $\text{H}_{2}\text{SO}_{4}$.
walkthrough:
See the second role of sulfuric acid**
With $\text{NaCl}$, concentrated $\text{H}_{2}\text{SO}_{4}$ simply donates a proton. But $\text{I}^{-}$ is a much stronger reducing agent than $\text{Cl}^{-}$, so the sulfuric acid also acts as an oxidiser.

Follow the unwanted oxidation**
Any $\text{HI}$ made is oxidised by the acid, for example to purple $\text{I}_{2}$ vapour plus $\text{SO}_{2}$ and water. That is why this route cannot be used to prepare pure HI, phosphoric acid is used instead.

Final answer: Concentrated $\text{H}_{2}\text{SO}_{4}$ is too strong an oxidising agent and oxidises $\text{I}^{-}$ / HI.
HI formed is oxidised further, so $\text{I}_{2}$ is formed instead of HI.

hints: Write $\Delta_{r}H = \sum \Delta_{f}H(\text{products}) - \sum \Delta_{f}H(\text{reactants})$ and remember $\Delta_{f}H$ of elements $\text{O}_{2}$ and $\text{Cl}_{2}$ is zero.
Multiply each $\Delta_{f}H$ by its stoichiometric number: $2$ for $\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$ and $4$ for HCl.
walkthrough:
Set up the formation sum**
For $$4\text{HCl(g)} + \text{O}_{2}\text{(g)} \rightleftharpoons 2\text{Cl}_{2}\text{(g)} + 2\text{H}_{2}\text{O(g)}$$ use $$\Delta_{r}H = \sum \Delta_{f}H(\text{products}) - \sum \Delta_{f}H(\text{reactants})$$ Elements in standard states have $\Delta_{f}H = 0$, so $\text{O}_{2}$ and $\text{Cl}_{2}$ contribute nothing.

Substitute and calculate**
$$\Delta_{r}H = [2 \times (-242)] - [4 \times (-92)]$$ $$= -484 - (-368) = -116\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$$ The negative sign shows the reaction is exothermic.

hints: Compare phases: reactants are gases while copper(II) chloride is a solid, so decide if the catalyst is in the same or different phase.
Recall the Boltzmann idea that lower activation energy means more molecules can react per second.
walkthrough:
Classify by phase**
All reactants and products are gases, $\text{HCl}$, $\text{O}_{2}$, $\text{Cl}_{2}$, $\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$, but copper(II) chloride is a solid. Different phase means heterogeneous catalysis, often with reaction on the surface.

Explain the rate effect**
A catalyst is not used up. It offers a different route with a lower activation energy barrier. At the same temperature many more molecules have energy greater than or equal to this lower barrier, so the rate increases.

Final answer: Heterogeneous catalyst, as $\text{CuCl}_{2}$ (solid) is in a different phase from the gaseous reactants.
It provides an alternative reaction pathway of lower activation energy, increasing rate.

hints: Use your value of $\Delta_{r}H = -116\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$ to decide which direction is exothermic.
Apply Le Chatelier: heating favours the endothermic direction to absorb the added heat.
walkthrough:
Identify the heat direction**
You found $\Delta_{r}H = -116\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$. Negative means the forward change $4\text{HCl} + \text{O}_{2} \rightarrow 2\text{Cl}_{2} + 2\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$ gives out heat, while the reverse takes heat in.

Predict the shift**
Raising temperature adds heat. The system opposes this by favouring the endothermic reverse reaction. So equilibrium moves left, leaving more $\text{HCl}$ and $\text{O}_{2}$ and less $\text{Cl}_{2}$ and $\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$ in the mixture.

Final answer: Forward reaction is exothermic ($\Delta_{r}H$ negative).
Increasing temperature to $1000^{\circ}\text{C}$ shifts equilibrium to the left, the endothermic direction, decreasing yield of $\text{Cl}_{2}$ and $\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$.

hints: Use stoichiometry $4:1:2:2$ with $0.600$ mol of $\text{Cl}_{2}$ formed to work out moles of HCl and $\text{O}_{2}$ used up.
Add all equilibrium moles to get total moles, then divide moles of $\text{Cl}_{2}$ by total to get mole fraction.
Use $p = \text{mole fraction} \times p_{\text{tot}}$ with $p_{\text{tot}} = 1.50 \times 10^{5}\text{ Pa}$.
walkthrough:
Find equilibrium moles by stoichiometry**
The equation is $$4\text{HCl} + \text{O}_{2} \rightarrow 2\text{Cl}_{2} + 2\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$$ Making $0.600$ mol $\text{Cl}_{2}$ must use $2 \times 0.600 = 1.20$ mol HCl and $0.600/2 = 0.300$ mol $\text{O}_{2}$. So left at equilibrium: $$n(\text{HCl}) = 1.60 - 1.20 = 0.400\text{ mol}$$ $$n(\text{O}_{2}) = 0.500 - 0.300 = 0.200\text{ mol}$$

Calculate mole fraction**
Total moles $= 0.400 + 0.200 + 0.600 + 0.600 = 1.80$ mol. Mole fraction $= \text{moles of gas} / \text{total moles}$, so $$x_{\text{Cl}_{2}} = \frac{0.600}{1.80} = 0.333$$

Convert to partial pressure**
Partial pressure $= \text{mole fraction} \times \text{total pressure}$, so $$p_{\text{Cl}_{2}} = 0.333 \times 1.50 \times 10^{5} = 5.00 \times 10^{4}\text{ Pa}$$

hints: Substitute the four partial pressures directly into $K_{p} = (p_{\text{Cl}_{2}})^{2}(p_{\text{H}_{2}\text{O}})^{2} / (p_{\text{HCl}})^{4}(p_{\text{O}_{2}})$ without converting units if all are in Pa.
Work out units by cancelling $\text{Pa}$ powers on top and bottom: $\text{Pa}^{4} / \text{Pa}^{5}$.
walkthrough:
Substitute into the given expression**
Put each value in Pa straight in: $$K_{p} = \frac{(3.6 \times 10^{4})^{2} \times (3.6 \times 10^{4})^{2}}{(4.8 \times 10^{4})^{4} \times 3.0 \times 10^{4}}$$ Numerator $= (3.6 \times 10^{4})^{4}$, denominator $= (4.8 \times 10^{4})^{4} \times 3.0 \times 10^{4}$. This gives $1.05 \times 10^{-5}$.

Deduce units**
Top has $\text{Pa}^{2} \times \text{Pa}^{2} = \text{Pa}^{4}$. Bottom has $\text{Pa}^{4} \times \text{Pa} = \text{Pa}^{5}$. So overall $\text{Pa}^{4-5} = \text{Pa}^{-1}$. Always include units for $K_{p}$ unless it is dimensionless.

hints: Recall that $K_{p}$ depends only on temperature, while a catalyst speeds up forward and reverse rates equally.
walkthrough:
Separate rate from position**
Removing the catalyst slows both forward and reverse reactions equally, so equilibrium is reached more slowly but the final partial pressures are unchanged. Since $K_{p}$ changes only with temperature, its value stays the same.
Final answer: $K_{p}$ would not change / stays the same, as catalysts do not affect position of equilibrium.
